successors.name: Roman Republic
successors.text: Cyrenaica as Ptolemy Apion left it: 'bequeathed it to the Roman Republic' in 96 BC, organised as a province by 78 BC (infobox 'Roman province (74 BC-643 AD)')

ledger.x: 332: The five Greek cities of the Cyrenaican Pentapolis, a republic since 440 on the page's infobox, submit to Alexander the Great.
332: The Pentapolis becomes a tributary of Alexander.
322: The Pentapolis ceases to be Macedon's tributary when Ptolemy's army takes it.
322: Ptolemy I's general Ophellas takes Cyrenaica.
About 305: the revolt of Cyrene against Ptolemy opens; Ptolemy's reaction is on the page only as the reconquest 'around 300 BC'.
About 300: Cyrenaica passes back to Ptolemy I's Egypt under the governor Magas.
276: Magas makes himself king of Cyrenaica.
Page silent: the page names the realm Cyrenaica and gives no border; Cliopatria's 272 outline is 62,000 km2 larger than the Pentapolis, with no other state on the added land.
246: Cyrenaica is reunited with Egypt when Berenice II, Magas' daughter, marries Ptolemy III.
145: Ptolemy VIII returns from Cyrene to be king of Egypt.
About 105: Ptolemy Apion is given Cyrene as a separate kingdom.
96: Ptolemy Apion dies and bequeaths Cyrenaica to Rome, which leaves it local administration until the province is organised.
74: The tributary Cyrenaica ends as Rome organises the province.
74: Rome annexes Cyrenaica as a province.
74: The last Cyrenaica, Apion's bequest, ends as a Roman province; Cliopatria draws the shape to 92, the bequest was in 96.

wars.name: Cyrenaean revolt against Ptolemy I
wars.outcome: The Cyrenaeans rebelled about 305 and Magas was sent about 300 to reconquer Cyrene; he stayed as governor to 276.

wars.name: Magas' war on Ptolemy II
wars.outcome: Magas 'was attacking Egypt from the west, as Antiochus I was attacking Palestine', married to Antiochus' daughter Apama II, but 'had to cancel his operations without results due to an internal revolt of the nomadic Libyan Marmaridae'; his later reign was…

certainty.note: No page gives a surveyed boundary; the coast cities are fixed, the desert edge and the Egyptian frontier are not.
